rationale: A broad scouting gradient ending at high organic strength should reveal all 10 compounds while retaining early peaks. The intermediate temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the current resolution margin remains. Keep the starting composition and temperature unchanged to isolate the effect of gradient slope.
Test lower-temperature selectivity at the faster gradient to separate the crowded central peaks. This isolates temperature as a potential way to restore resolution without extending the gradient.
Lower temperature worsened several separations, so test higher temperature at the same gradient slope. This may improve central-peak selectivity while further shortening retention.

Test an intermediate temperature to balance the central-pair separation gained at 55 C against the new close pair that appeared there. Keep the fast gradient unchanged to preserve the zero time penalty.

Modestly lengthen the gradient at 55 C to try to resolve its single deficient pair while retaining the favorable temperature selectivity. The last peak should still elute early enough to avoid a time penalty.

Reduce the gradient slope slightly further to bring the remaining close pair above R = 1.5. The estimated last-peak time is near 8 minutes, potentially giving full resolution with little or no time penalty.

Test a slightly steeper gradient than injection 7 to shorten retention while aiming to preserve the maximum CRF. The small slope increase should leave both critical pairs above R = 1.5 and provide more margin below the time-penalty threshold.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a higher starting organic fraction at the same slope as injection 7 for a potentially faster alternative. This probes whether full resolution can be retained with more margin below the time-penalty threshold.

Flatten the gradient at the higher starting composition to recover the separation lost in injection 9. This tests whether the maximum CRF can be maintained with a different balance of retention time and critical-pair resolution.

Test a lower starting organic fraction with a steeper gradient to strengthen the separation that deteriorated at phi0 = 0.15 while keeping elution fast. Monitor the other central pair to see whether this provides another maximum-score method.

Slightly flatten injection 11's gradient to raise its remaining deficient separation above R = 1.5 while aiming to preserve the other critical pair. This could match the maximum CRF with a shorter last-peak time than injection 7.

Test a slightly shallower gradient adjacent to injection 12 to map the maximum-score region. This should improve the earlier critical separation, while checking whether the later pair remains above R = 1.5 without a time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test the temperature sensitivity of injection 13 by increasing only T. Higher temperature may improve its marginal central separation and shorten retention, but could compromise the earlier critical pair.

With the maximum score already secured, explore a faster high-temperature method at higher starting organic strength. This may move the temperature-sensitive pair through its selectivity crossover into a resolved reversed order, though early-peak compression is a risk.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve early-peak retention, while steepening the gradient to test separation on the reversed-order side of the temperature-sensitive crossover. This explores a faster alternative to the methods already achieving maximum CRF.

Steepen the gradient at the same starting composition and temperature to test whether the remaining close pair separates further after its order reversal. This could yield a faster maximum-score method, although compression of the other central separations is a risk.

Return to the maximum-score region with a slightly shallower gradient than injection 7. This should preserve full resolution and may still avoid a time penalty, while testing a higher final organic strength for column washout.

Match injection 12's successful gradient slope with a shorter programmed gradient and lower endpoint. All peaks previously eluted before this gradient would finish at the outlet, so the maximum CRF should be preserved.

Use injection 7's successful gradient slope with an earlier endpoint, still after the last peak's expected outlet elution. This should preserve its maximum CRF and resolution margin with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a slightly shallower gradient beside the established maximum-score region to improve the earlier critical separation. The later critical pair should remain resolved, while the last peak is expected near 8.3 minutes with little or no time penalty.
Probe the steeper boundary of the maximum-score region between injections 6 and 8. This should shorten retention slightly, while testing whether the earlier critical pair still meets R = 1.5.

Preserve the successful gradient slope of injections 12 and 19 while extending the endpoint to 0.95 organic. Because all peaks should elute before the endpoint changes their solvent exposure, this alternative is expected to retain the maximum CRF.

Test a gradient slope between the maximum-score methods of injections 12 and 13. This should preserve full resolution and zero time penalty while further defining the range of methods achieving CRF 1.000.

Use the final injection to probe the shallower-gradient boundary of the maximum-score region. Full resolution is expected, with the last peak near 8.4 minutes testing where the time penalty begins; injection 7 already secures the maximum CRF.
